The video editing process is an intricate combination of multiple steps, including
importing footage, defining shot boundaries, adding transitions, determining a
sequence of shots, and fine-tuning the overall layout. Despite its complexity,
researchers have primarily focused on a single step, such as identifying shot
boundaries, leaving the rest of the editing process to be tackled manually.
This paper presents a comprehensive dataset, known as the Video Editing Dataset
(VED), which addresses this gap by providing a detailed, pixel-level
characterization of each step in the video editing process. Leveraging this
dataset, we establish a benchmark suite to investigate the current capabilities
of AI-assisted video editing, and we find that current techniques are limited to
only a few tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that AI-assisted editing can be
significantly improved by integrating the knowledge from our annotated dataset. 
The dataset and benchmark suite are publicly available at
https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/VED/. The project also includes a
user-friendly video editing application that utilizes our research. 
The application is available at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/VEDApp/. 
The VED dataset is being used to host the 2022 PASCAL Visual Grounding
Challenge, which aims to advance the state-of-the-art in video editing. 
The challenge's results will be presented at the CVPR 2022.

which aims to provide an introductory tutorial on the current limitations and
opportunities in video editing.

genres, encompassing 12 categories and over 1.5 million linked mentions to over
400,000 Wikipedia articles. In contrast to existing entity linking datasets,

domain. The creation of WikiGUM involved processing over 4.5 million Wikipedia

experiments on public datasets reveal that existing linkers struggle to generalize
their performance across various genres, underscoring the need for a more
comprehensive dataset like WikiGUM to advance the field of entity linking. The
dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/ylee-lab/wikigum. For more

Deep neural networks typically require a large number of parameters to achieve high accuracy, but this can be mitigated by compact features that are learned early in the training process. However, compact features often come at the cost of low performance. To address this trade-off, we propose a new approach called In-training Representation Alignment (IRA), which aligns the compact features extracted at different layers during training to improve the performance without increasing the number of parameters. By aligning the compact features, we can achieve performance comparable to using full features while reducing the number of parameters. Additionally, we can stack multiple compact features to further improve the performance. Experimental results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters. For example, we can achieve 76.8% top-1 ImageNet accuracy using only 0.3 million parameters, a 2.4-fold reduction compared to the baseline. The code will be publicly available after acceptance. We also show that our approach can be used to improve the performance of existing compact models by fine-tuning the compact features. Furthermore, we can use our approach to reduce the number of parameters in existing models by feature pruning, achieving 76.4% top-1 ImageNet accuracy using only 0.15 million parameters. The exponential growth in scientific literature has made it increasingly difficult for researchers to stay current on the latest developments in their field. As a result, they are often overwhelmed by the sheer volume of articles available, with hundreds of thousands being published every year. To mitigate this issue, a literature recommender system has been proposed to suggest relevant articles that readers may have overlooked. To this end, a novel approach has been developed, utilizing a neural network-based recommender system that incorporates attention mechanisms and embedding techniques to capture the complex relationships between authors, articles, and keywords. The system has been trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 3.5 million articles from leading scientific publishers and has demonstrated promising results, with a high success rate of 0.9 for medium-sized article collections. To further refine its performance, a hybrid approach has been proposed, combining the neural network's output with a probabilistic model-based method. The hybrid model has shown exceptional accuracy, with a high success rate of 0.85 for medium-sized article collections. To facilitate widespread adoption, a user-friendly web interface has been developed, providing seamless access to the recommender system and the underlying data analysis. Experimental results indicate that Ladder effectively fortifies DNNs against diverse types of attacks, including those that exploit their internal internal latent boundaries. Furthermore, the method exhibits resilience against unseen attacks, including a variant of the PGD attack that we developed, while also demonstrating impressive performance on benchmark adversarial robustness datasets. The use of multiple sites for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging connectivity analysis has become widespread, but the significance of this approach in statistical power and prediction accuracy remains unclear. This study compares the predictive performance of local and multisite models in statistical simulations, examining their sensitivity to varying sample sizes and network sizes. Results show that multisite models consistently outperform local models in terms of predictive accuracy, but their sensitivity to sample size is comparable. A separate empirical analysis involving 1,000 functional magnetic resonance imaging datasets from the Human Connectome Project reveals that multisite models are capable of achieving comparable prediction performance with a fourth of the required samples. Overall, our findings suggest that multisite models are more effective for predictive applications, but may be less sensitive to sample size in the estimation of connectivity matrices. This study underscores the importance of considering the specific application in the choice of model when working with functional magnetic resonance imaging data. techniques for enhancing model performance. This study also evaluates the
importance of image quality in bird species classification and suggests future
directions for research. Our experiments utilized a large dataset of 50 bird

on a large dataset of images and then using the trained model to generate new
images for further training. Our results demonstrate the potential benefits of
this method in improving bird species classification accuracy. Our study is
the first to investigate the role of transfer learning and multistage training
in bird species classification. Our findings are intended to contribute to the
development of advanced machine learning models for bird species classification.

GANs have become a preferred solution for data generation, but their training can be complicated by a common problem known as mode collapse, which occurs when the model fails to capture the diverse range of data modes. To address this challenge, we investigate mode collapse from a new perspective, examining how it relates to the underlying structure of the data distribution. Our research introduces a novel metric, the relative scale of the smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), to analyze the scale of data modes and assess mode collapse risk. By using this metric, we analyze mode collapse in various GAN architectures, including StyleGAN2, BigGAN, and DCGAN. Our results show that the mode collapse problem is more severe in DCGAN compared to the other two models. Furthermore, we find that the mode collapse issue in DCGAN arises from the model's tendency to converge to a local optimum prematurely, which can be mitigated by adjusting the learning rate. Our research also reveals that the relative scale of the smallest eigenvalue of the FIM can be used to predict mode collapse risk, and we provide a theoretical explanation for this connection. Additionally, we demonstrate that the mode collapse problem can be mitigated by using a novel loss function that encourages the model to capture a broader range of data modes. Our findings are supported by both qualitative and quantitative analyses, and we believe that this research opens up new avenues for investigating mode collapse in GANs. The primary challenge in assessing the quality of dehazed images lies in the absence of a reference image. This study aims to address this problem by introducing a new quality metric for evaluating dehazed images, which we refer to as the Partial Discrepancy Metric. The Partial Discrepancy Metric is based on the observation that the region surrounding the haze region is less relevant for image quality evaluation. To account for this, we propose a novel loss function that measures the difference between a dehazed image and its original, distorted version. The loss function is optimized using a gradient descent algorithm, which enables us to obtain a new, reference-free dehazed image. The quality of the dehazed image is then evaluated by comparing it with its original, distorted counterpart. Our experiments demonstrate that the Partial Discrepancy Metric outperforms existing metrics on both objective and subjective grounds. The proposed method is also computationally efficient, with a running time of less than a minute on a single GPU. The class imbalance problem is widespread in real-world datasets, where instances from the minority class are scarce and difficult to obtain labeled supervision for. As a result, researchers have turned to Positive-Unlabeled learning (PUNL) to overcome the limitations of class imbalance. However, PUNL requires a significant amount of time-consuming and expensive data collection to obtain the necessary positive samples. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Self-supervised PUNL (PUNL-SS), which leverages self-supervised pre-training to effectively tackle the class imbalance issue. Our proposed method involves a self-supervised pre-training phase that utilizes pseudo labels generated from a pre-trained model, followed by a fine-tuning phase that uses these pseudo labels to train a classifier. We also introduce a novel loss function called Self-Supervised Contrastive Loss (SSCL) that helps to overcome the limitations of PUNL by utilizing the self-supervised features. Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that PUNL-SS outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance and efficiency. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of PUNL-SS that highlights its advantages over PUNL. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/Ankush2020/PUNL-SS. Recent studies have highlighted the need to create adversarial samples that are indistinguishable from genuine data in visual recognition tasks. Current methods, however, are limited in their ability to generate such samples across diverse categories. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that enables the production of unrestricted adversarial samples by replacing non-semantic visual features. By employing a semantic feature disentanglement network, we can isolate meaningful and non-meaningful features within an input image. Adversarial samples are then generated by replacing non-meaningful features with those from other classes, resulting in images that are visually similar yet semantically distinct. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in producing unrestricted adversarial samples that are nearly indistinguishable from genuine data. Additionally, we show that our method can be integrated into existing black-box attacks to improve their efficacy. Our proposed method is theoretically sound and experimentally effective, outperforming existing ensemble Q-learning techniques in various scenarios, including episodic and episodic-transient environments. that enables efficient processing of large point clouds in a single step. By utilizing

methods in semantic segmentation, achieving a 2.5% increase in mIoU score. Additionally,

outpacing previous methods by 2.5-4.5% in average mAP and 1.5-2.5% in average recall.

The effectiveness of unsupervised clustering methods relies on their ability to provide meaningful insights into the underlying data structure. However, the interpretation of clustering results can be compromised when objects from distinct categories are grouped together. To achieve a better understanding of the cluster outcomes, a new approach called the Cluster Interpretability Metric (CIM) is proposed. By analyzing the connectivity of the cluster graph, the CIM score measures the extent to as a cluster's internal connections compare to its connections with other clusters. Through theoretical analysis, the properties of the CIM score are established, and it is shown that a linear relationship exists between the CIM score and the clustering quality. To balance the trade-off between clustering quality and interpretability, a new clustering algorithm called the Linearly Interpretable Clustering (LIC) method is introduced. By incorporating the CIM score into the clustering objective, the LIC method automatically adjusts the clustering quality based on the required level of interpretability. Experimental results demonstrate that the LIC method outperforms existing clustering algorithms in terms of interpretability. Moreover, the LIC method is also effective in identifying meaningful clusters in complex datasets. Fake news detection research has gained significant attention due to the dissemination of misleading information on social media. However, current fake news detection methods rely heavily on manually labeled data, which is scarce and expensive to obtain. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to automatically generate propaganda-loaded training data. By leveraging a pre-trained language model and a text generator, we create a synthetic dataset of fake news articles. These synthetic articles exhibit high levels of propaganda, as measured by a proposed propaganda score. We evaluate the effectiveness of our generated data by comparing it with authentic fake news articles. The results show that the synthetic data can be used as a substitute for the real thing and can even improve the performance of machine learning models when used in conjunction with a small amount of genuine data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our generated data can be used to fine-tune language models, which can subsequently be used to identify genuine fake news articles. The proposed approach has the potential to significantly reduce the cost and effort required to obtain high-quality training data for fake news detection. Our findings indicate that the most effective attack, DeepFool, can create adversarial data that closely resembles the original data, making it difficult to detect even by humans. Pedestrian anonymization, a technique for protecting individual privacy, has been widely adopted in surveillance systems. However, existing methods that utilize GAN-based anonymization have significant drawbacks, including the potential for high visual distortion, which could compromise their practicality. Moreover, these methods often rely on pre-trained pedestrian detection models, which can be vulnerable to attacks and may pose a risk to personal privacy. To address these issues, we introduce a novel GAN-based anonymization framework that is designed to be privacy-preserving. By integrating anonymization and pedestrian detection into a single training process, we can ensure that the anonymization method remains secure. Additionally, we propose a novel loss function that enables the GAN to generate images with high quality while maintaining anonymity. Through extensive testing on various datasets, we demonstrate that our approach can achieve a balance between privacy preservation and visual quality. Despite its popularity, tools lack the ability to identify the parts of a property that are responsible for a specification's incompatibility. This limitation is addressed by introducing the first algorithm for computing the core of an LTLf property that makes a specification incompatible. This innovative method is based on a translation into the more manageable monadic second-order logic of propositional logic with first-order elements and uses an original model checking technique. Furthermore, it offers a new approach to model checking for monadic second-order logic with one free variable. The effectiveness of the algorithm is demonstrated through its integration into the open-source tool Satspec, which can also handle traditional LTL properties. Experimental results show that the computed cores are significantly smaller than those produced by other existing tools. We introduce a novel computational approach for solving the fractional Schrödinger equation on an infinite scale. By translating this equation into a pseudodifferential equation, we derive a corresponding integral operator that is well-suited for fast Fourier transformation. We then develop a spectral approximation method for this operator, which we demonstrate to be highly effective through numerical experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed method is well-suited for parallelized computation, further enhancing its practical applications. To facilitate future research, we provide a comprehensive MATLAB code for our method. Finally, we discuss potential future research directions and avenues for exploration. This paper introduces DARE, a comprehensive handwritten date recognition system, which was developed within the EU HOSFA project framework. The system is designed to process handwritten dates, determine if they are legitimate, and if so, return them in standard format. DARE consists of three primary components: a recognition module, a validity checker, and a integration module. A unified framework is employed, utilizing a single HOG-SVM classifier for both recognition and validity assessment, which are then combined at the integration level. This research introduces a novel approach to optimizing Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) configurations for speaker verification tasks by leveraging machine learning. In recent years, researchers have increasingly turned to deep learning methods for inference in graphical models, but these approaches often come with a price: they require large amounts of labeled data to train, making them inaccessible to researchers without access to such resources. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method for approximate inference in graphical models using a mean field inference algorithm that leverages graph attention networks. Our method, which is based on the idea of using a neural network to optimize the mean field approximation process, offers several advantages over existing approaches, including the ability to handle complex energy functions and the potential to improve the accuracy of inference without requiring additional labeled data. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a series of experiments on several benchmark datasets, including a synthetic dataset, the MNIST handwritten digit recognition task, and the COCO image segmentation task. The results of these experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and speed, while also requiring fewer hyperparameters to tune. Moreover, we found that our method is able to handle energy functions with higher clique sizes than other mean field inference algorithms, while achieving better results on the COCO image segmentation task. This study investigates the feasibility of using satellite remote sensing to accurately estimate crop production in pre-harvest periods. We developed an early estimation method for rice and maize production in Senegal through a combination of crop mapping, area calculation, and yield prediction. We then compared this approach with traditional production estimates from a well-established agricultural survey conducted by the Senegalese Ministry of Agriculture. Our results show that while the early estimation method provides less accurate production forecasts, it still offers precise estimates of annual production levels that align with the Ministry's survey results. Furthermore, this method enables the prediction of production trends over time, which was not possible using the traditional survey-based approach. Our findings have significant implications for the early detection of production risks, crisis management, and long-term planning in Senegal's agricultural sector. The methodology presented here can be adapted for early crop production predictions in other West African countries as well. Our research also highlights the potential of using satellite remote sensing for crop production estimation in other regions of the world. The full details of our research, including data, methods, and results, can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/GeoSpatials/production_estimation_from_remote_sensing. The solvation free energy of drugs exposed to supercritical CO2 plays a crucial role in various industrial applications, such as SFC separations. However, accurately determining this energy using computer simulations is complicated due to the high molecular complexity and CO2's non-ideal behavior. Researchers have developed alternative methods to estimate this energy using molecular simulations, which involve different levels of complexity and CO2 treatment. They employed these methods on a set of diverse drugs to evaluate their performance and CO2 treatment approaches. The results showed that including CO2's non-ideal behavior significantly improved estimates, particularly when incorporating specific anisotropic interactions. However, achieving accurate results required precise CO2 treatment, which may not be feasible for all simulations. The most accurate method involved using a complex solvation model with a specific CO2 treatment, while a simpler method using a different solvation model produced acceptable results with a less complex CO2 treatment. The results demonstrated that estimating solvation free energies in supercritical environments is complex and requires careful consideration of various factors, including the solvent and treatment of the compressed phase. The adoption of a feature toggle (FT) has become a prominent best practice in software development, enabling the simultaneous release of different features to different user groups without requiring strict version control. However, the extent to which FTs reduce the frequency of branch merges and defects in open-source software remains an open question. Our analysis of 1,221 open-source Java projects from GitHub revealed that the use of FTs does not significantly impact branch merges and that there is no notable difference in defect rates between FT-using and non-FT-using projects. Our findings suggest that the use of FTs does not provide a competitive advantage in terms of quality. Our results are consistent with the idea that experienced developers adopt FTs as a result of their past struggles with integration and testing, rather than for their supposed benefits. This implies that the primary advantage of FTs may lie in improving the efficiency of the development process, rather than necessarily reducing the frequency of defects. Our research highlights the need for further investigation into the relationship between FT adoption and quality metrics in software development. Future studies could explore the relationship between FT adoption and other quality metrics, such as code complexity and test coverage, to shed more light on the topic. when data is scarce. To overcome this challenge, a novel approach involves 
creating a meta-filter that can identify and filter out irrelevant information.

supervised method to learn the task at hand and then using an unsupervised

more efficient and effective few-shot learning model, one that can quickly 
adapt to new tasks without requiring extensive data or computational 
resources. Experimental results demonstrate the success of this approach, 
yielding performance comparable to the current best methods while requiring 
significantly less data and reducing computation time by a substantial margin. 
Moreover, this approach can be easily integrated into existing few-shot 
learning models, making it a versatile solution for a wide range of problems.

The phenomenon of emotional transmission, where people observe the emotions of others and adopt those emotions, has been extensively studied in both social science and psychology. However, prior research has been limited by its focus on isolated, static observations and neglect of the complex dynamics involved. In this research, we develop a novel method for measuring the spread of emotions within dynamic social networks, using Twitter data and analyzing over 1.5 million tweets and 1.6 million retweets across various topics and emotions. Our results demonstrate that our approach can accurately identify the emotional contagion effect and has potential applications in fields such as marketing and public health. Furthermore, our findings suggest that emotions are more easily transmitted within social networks than in isolated, one-on-one interactions, and that certain types of relationships, such as those between friends, are more conducive to emotional contagion. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the likelihood of emotional transmission decreases as the distance between individuals increases. Finally, our work highlights the importance of considering the dynamic nature of social networks in estimating the spread of emotions, and the need for future research to explore the underlying psychological mechanisms involved. This study presents a novel approach to reinforcement learning, grounded in active inference, which enables an agent to learn a policy by optimizing its beliefs about the environment's state. The policy is formulated as a prior over actions, and the agent iteratively refines this policy through a two-stage process: first, it updates its expectations about the environment's state by selecting actions and observing their outcomes, and second, it updates the policy based on its expectations. The proposed method is tested in various scenarios, including simple gridworlds, finding that it effectively learns optimal policies for tasks with both discrete and continuous action spaces. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated in scenarios where the optimal policy is known, highlighting the method's potential for learning in complex, partially observed environments. In recent years, deep learning has become a crucial tool for handling complex data types, but it also raises significant concerns about data privacy. To address these issues, we propose an innovative approach that ensures both the confidentiality of sensitive data and the preservation of useful information. Our method involves using an autoencoder to create a probabilistic representation of data, which is then utilized to generate a transformed dataset that prioritizes utility over privacy. To further enhance data privacy, we employ a deep adversarial network to introduce noise into the probabilistic representation, resulting in a transformed dataset that effectively balances both utility and confidentiality. Our approach has been successfully tested on various datasets, including images and videos, with diverse data types. The results demonstrate that the transformed data maintains the essential characteristics of the original data while significantly reducing the likelihood of identifying individual instances. Moreover, we found that the transformed data maintains the same classification accuracy as the original data, indicating that our method is effective in preserving the utility of the data while also protecting individual instances. This research paper introduces SART - Similarity, Analogies, and Relatedness for Tatar,
a comprehensive evaluation dataset tailored for Tatar language word embeddings.
The dataset comprises three primary components: SART-Sim, a similarity assessment,
a comprehensive analogies challenge, and a relatedness test SART-Related.
SART-Sim and SART-Related draw inspiration from datasets developed for Russian,
Arabic, and other languages, while SART-Analog from the English language.
The SART dataset contains 1,821,919 word embeddings of 1,821,919 Tatar words,
generated from Tatar Wikipedia and sourced from the Universal Dependency database.
The SART dataset is freely accessible online and can be utilized for evaluating
Tatar word embeddings across a variety of tasks and models. The SART dataset also
includes a baseline evaluation of word embeddings generated by prominent Tatar word embedding models. The results indicate that current word embedding models are still inadequate in capturing the inherent semantic meaning of Tatar words. The SART dataset is anticipated to facilitate the development of more advanced Tatar word embeddings and serve as a catalyst for the creation of Tatar language NLP resources. A crucial step in compacting large neural networks is pruning, which involves
reducing their size by eliminating unessential parameters. Traditional pruning
methods involve a fixed percentage or threshold-based reduction of parameters,
resulting in minor changes to the network's architecture. This paper introduces a
novel pruning approach, which dynamically allocates a pruning budget to the
parameters, allowing the network to decide how to utilize the resources. We
formulate this process as a mathematical optimization problem and develop a
pruning algorithm that iteratively assigns and reallocate parameters.

state-of-the-art performance on various tasks, including image classification and
language modeling. Notably, our approach yields a significant reduction in model
size, which can be seen as a form of compression. The accompanying code is

The way people interact with visual information is deeply ingrained, and it's likely that our brain's response to visual cues is automatic and instantaneous. This study investigates how setting a time limit for making judgments about image shapes affects how people focus on those shapes. A filtering system allows a constant number of fixed-size key-value pairs to efficiently store a sequence of items, processing each in a single pass. This versatile tool has numerous applications across databases, caching systems, and scientific research. This study focuses on optimizing the support optimality filter, a variant that prioritizes the most frequent items, and we propose a new solution called the adaptive cuckoo filter. By leveraging a unique combination of cuckoo space and dynamic sliding windows, our filter achieves optimal performance, supporting the filtering of a sequence of $k$ items with a time complexity of $O(k \log k)$ and space complexity of $O(k \log \log k)$. Furthermore, our filter boasts a practical advantage of requiring only a single memory allocation, a key benefit in various real-world scenarios. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our filter in both static and dynamic environments. Notably, our filter surpasses existing solutions in both space efficiency and support optimality, and it outperforms them in terms of lookup speed as well. Additionally, our filter exhibits superior performance in handling sequential queries, and it surpasses existing solutions in terms of adaptability to the query sequence. Finally, our filter demonstrates exceptional performance in real-world applications, outperforming existing solutions in various database and caching scenarios. This study showcases the potential of our filter in real-world applications, and we believe that it will serve as a valuable addition to the existing repertoire of filtering systems. Semi-supervised learning has been widely adopted in computer vision tasks, but current methods often rely on a single stage of supervised and unsupervised learning, neglecting the potential benefits of a more structured approach. To address this, a new technique called FlexMatch is proposed, leveraging curriculum learning to enhance semi-supervised vision tasks. FlexMatch employs a two-stage process, initially utilizing a teacher-student framework to generate pseudo labels, then refining these labels through a second iteration with a progressively improved student. The approach is flexible, allowing for either fixed or dynamic progression between stages, and can be easily integrated into existing semi-supervised learning methods. When applied to image classification tasks, FlexMatch demonstrates improved performance over existing methods, and can also be adapted for object detection tasks, showcasing its versatility and potential for further application in semi-supervised learning scenarios. Federated learning, a highly effective approach to maintaining user privacy, has seen widespread adoption. However, the current methods often rely on a single global model that fails to account for varying data distributions across different users. This can lead to compromised performance, particularly when models are adapted to a single distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel personalized federated learning framework that leverages hypernetworks, allowing each user to have a unique model tailored to its specific data distribution. Additionally, we propose an innovative optimization technique that enables users to collaborate in adapting their personalized models. Our framework's potential is showcased through its application in medical image segmentation tasks, where it outperforms existing methods by achieving higher average and lowest standard deviation in performance across users. This demonstrates the framework's ability to strike a better balance between user privacy and performance. Our experiments also highlight the effectiveness of hypernetworks in model adaptation, with the use of hypernetworks resulting in improved performance compared to other methods. Furthermore, we find that the proposed framework's performance is highly robust and consistent across users, with the lowest standard deviation in performance among all methods tested. This suggests that the framework's ability to learn user-specific models effectively. Our framework's source code is available for public review. The increasing demand for conversational agents in healthcare has led to a surge in research on using natural language processing to identify medical symptoms. In 1930, Menger introduced the concept of a "circle domain," which is essentially a convex set of points in a plane where every pair of points is connected by a circle within this set. Two years later, he posed two problems: first, whether such a set must be a disk; and second, whether a similar set in three dimensions would necessarily be a sphere. In this paper, the authors provide a negative response to these questions, demonstrating that both assumptions can be relaxed. Specifically, they show that in a circle domain where every pair of points is connected by a circle, the opposite ends of these circles must intersect within this domain. We introduce Fuel, a practical and efficient compiler framework that implements 
value-based memory safety features, initially developed as a part of the 
Futhark high-level high-performance programming language. Fuel's capabilities 
extend beyond Futhark, supporting any low-level memory-managed language with 
optional result typing. Result typing enables explicit type annotations for 
function results, essential for certain performance optimizations. Fuel's 
approach to result typing is unique in that it is optional, adaptable, and 
backward-compatible with existing code. We showcase Fuel's functionality by 
integrating it with the Cranelang ecosystem, utilizing it to compile 
intermediate code to safe, result-typed machine code. Fuel's performance is 
competitive with hand-coded assembly code, and its framework is extensible, 
enabling users to add new memory safety features as needed. Fuel's source code 
is available for public access at https://github.com/marcelo-fonseca/fuel. A 
detailed design document is also available at https://crane.io/docs/fuel-design.pdf.

Fonseca Ferreira, and it is his academic thesis project under the supervision 
of Andy Lowe. The project is a collaboration between the University of 
Copenhagen and the Cranelang team. Finally, Fuel is released under the Apache 2 
License. For further information, please do not hesitate to contact the author.

To address this issue, researchers have developed techniques such as channel normalization and speaker separation to mitigate the effects of overlapped speech, but they often come with a significant computational cost. This paper presents a novel approach to estimating the dynamic states of power networks, which are modeled using complex differential and algebraic equations. Notably, the simulations were conducted using a custom power network model, which is based on real-world data from a local US utility. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed analysis of the estimation accuracy, highlighting the impact of measurement noise and parameter uncertainties on state estimation performance. Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms a traditional Kalman filter approach in scenarios involving noisy measurements and uncertain parameters. Moreover, the paper presents a comparative study, which reveals that the proposed method is computationally more efficient than a competing nonlinear filter approach. Finally, the paper provides an overview of potential applications of the proposed method in power system control and monitoring. This includes a case study demonstrating how the method can be used to develop control strategies for voltage and reactive power management. Another case study illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in detecting anomalies in power grid performance. Overall, the paper presents a significant contribution to the field of nonlinear filtering for power system modeling. We utilize the Financial Sentence Parser to create a comprehensive database of over 1.3 million news headlines and company statements, which we then use to train a word embedding model. Our model is applied to forecast volatility for the S&P 500 index via two distinct methods: direct prediction using the learned embeddings, and prediction of a volatility proxy variable, SVI, by mapping embeddings onto SVI. This study presents a novel robotic manipulation technique that enables a robot
to independently move objects without prior knowledge of their internal structure.
A key innovation of our approach is an algorithm that uses a particle-based
model to predict the movement of individual particles within an object, allowing
the robot to make decisions based on these simulations. By comparing simulated
outcomes to actual object movements, the robot can adapt its simulation parameters
and develop a more accurate model of the object's internal particles. Our method
enables robots to successfully manipulate objects with complex internal structures
without prior knowledge, as demonstrated through simulations and physical
experiments. Our approach is the first to demonstrate effective object manipulation
without relying on pre-existing knowledge of an object's internal structure. Our
code and data are publicly available for review. For more information on this
research, visit https://sites.google.com/berkeley.edu/particle-based-manipulation.

Go's growing popularity as a scalable language necessitates effective tools for detecting and debugging concurrency issues.  While existing methods for Go concurrency bug detection are limited, they often struggle with false positives and high execution times.  In response, we introduce BinGo, a binary analysis tool that leverages lightweight runtime instrumentation and efficient data analysis to identify Go concurrency bugs.  By focusing on the runtime binary, BinGo bypasses the need for source code access or runtime execution, allowing it to pinpoint bugs with high accuracy and minimal false positives.  Our evaluation demonstrates BinGo's effectiveness, as it successfully detects 90% of bugs in the Go Test Suite and outperforms a leading tool by 1-2 orders of magnitude in performance.  Furthermore, we showcase BinGo's ability to identify issues in real-world open-source projects.  Our results are available at https://sites.google.com/view binge research. However, the high overhead of feedback in mMTC combined with the limited capabilities of user equipment makes uplink feedback a challenging task. By utilizing a compressed sensing algorithm, the base station is able to recover the channel state from uplink signals. To further improve the accuracy of channel state estimation, a deep learning-based fusion network is introduced that integrates the channel state from uplink signals with the channel state from downlink signals. As a result, the proposed approach is able to achieve a significant reduction in normalized mean square error (NMSE) compared to existing methods. Simulation results confirm that the proposed approach is able to achieve a NMSE of 10^-3 with a substantial reduction in feedback overhead of 10^3 bits. Moreover, the proposed approach is shown to be effective in scenarios with both perfect and imperfect reciprocity between uplink and downlink channels. By leveraging the knowledge of channel reciprocity, the fusion network is able to achieve a significant improvement in the accuracy of channel state estimation. The proposed approach is thus well-suited for use in mMTC applications where there are strict limitations on feedback overhead and reciprocity between uplink and downlink channels is not always known. Consequently, we propose a novel approach to this task, which involves training a conversational agent to generate responses that are both consistent with a user's persona and supported by relevant knowledge. Call graph analytics for software maintenance and evolution has been a growing area of interest. However, existing call graph analytics tools are limited in their ability to capture the dynamics of evolving systems. To address this, we've developed a new approach, EVOMETER, which extracts and analyzes call graphs from version to version to identify evolving patterns. EVOMETER's core functionality includes call graph comparison, subgraph identification, and evolution distance calculation, which can be used to pinpoint performance issues, optimize dependencies, and facilitate refactoring. As a proof of concept, we've applied EVOMETER to the Linux kernel, demonstrating its capacity to capture and analyze evolving call graphs within software ecosystems. The limitations of our approach are also explored, which may lead to future research avenues in this field. EVOMETER's source code is publicly available on GitHub. The approach is demonstrated through the characterization of stable finite time blowups for the parabolic equation $u_t=\text{det}D^2f(Du)$, where a blowup profile is constructed given certain conditions on the function $f$. Notably, these conditions can be seen as a consequence of the level set formulation of partial uniform ellipticity. The approach also yields new results for second-order nonlinear elliptic equations, including the monotonicity formula for the first eigenvalue of the $p$-Laplacian and the characterization of its blowup profiles. The multi-modal fusion stage in brain tumor segmentation is often hindered by 
the limitations of available modalities. To address this issue, we introduce 
MissModSynFUSION, a novel approach that synthesizes missing modalities in real-time 
for improved brain tumor segmentation. By utilizing a novel generative model, 
we can generate any required modality for a specific input. To optimize this 
process, we employ a multi-task learning framework that enables the model to 
learn feature representations for various modalities. Subsequently, we apply 
a fusion module to combine the generated and original modalities, ensuring 
that the synthesized features are realistic and beneficial for segmentation. 
Furthermore, we propose a modality-level attention mechanism to dynamically 
assign varying weights to different modalities, allowing for more effective 
segmentation. Through comprehensive experiments on the BraTS Challenge, 
MissModSynFION has demonstrated superior performance compared to other methods, 
achieving a Dice score of 0.83 and Hausdorff distance of 12.8mm. The project page is available at https://github.com/zhengjunshuai/MissModSynFUSION. 
The code and models used in this study will be made available after publication. 
This work will be presented at MICCAI 2022. To facilitate future research, 
we will maintain a dedicated website with pre-trained models and code. 
The website is accessible at https://sites.google.com/view/missmodfusion. 
The results of MissModSynFION are expected to serve as a valuable resource for 
brain tumor segmentation and missing modality synthesis research.

This study presents a computational algorithm for calculating standardized residuals within multivariate autoregressive structural time series models. These residuals hold significant theoretical importance in analyzing complex time series dynamics, as they can be leveraged to derive critical model insights. Given the complexity and computational demands of MARSS models, a robust and efficient method is necessary to extract meaningful information from the residuals. The proposed algorithm utilizes state-space methods to calculate the posterior precision matrix for the residuals, and subsequently, computes the standardized residuals through a single call of a linear solver. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through a range of numerical experiments, and its practical applications are further illustrated in the analysis of real-world data sets. The algorithm's implementation and accompanying data sets can be accessed via the open-source software packages MARSS and tsDyn on the CRAN platform. The MARSS package includes a detailed description of the algorithm, and the tsDyn package provides a comprehensive overview of the MARSS model. The study also explores the potential applications of standardized residuals in the context of financial market analysis, and highlights the significance of the residuals in the analysis of economic indicators. However, existing techniques for detecting these tunnels have limitations when it comes to MPLS, particularly in online applications that require precise timing. These approaches typically rely on indirect methods such as network scanning and tracing, which can be time-consuming and may not always yield accurate results. Moreover, some methods rely on vulnerable server-side code that may expose private information or compromise security. In this research, a novel technique called TNT is proposed to directly identify MPLS tunnels using only client-side data and minimal network access. TNT achieves this by analyzing packet patterns and analyzing the structure of the tunnel, which allows it to detect tunnels in real-time without requiring server cooperation. Additionally, TNT can be easily integrated into existing network monitoring tools to provide real-time tunnel detection. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of TNT in detecting previously unknown tunnels in popular applications, which can be traced even after the application has been terminated. In contrast to existing techniques, TNT does not require tracing or scanning, which can be time-consuming and may not always yield accurate results. Moreover, TNT does not require any modifications to the network or applications, which can be a significant advantage in terms of deployment and scalability. In comparison, TNT outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and speed, which can be a significant advantage in the context of MPLS tunnel detection. The complexity of software systems is growing due to their widespread use across various applications, making it challenging to configure and tailor them to individual needs. As a result, software systems often have a vast configuration space that users struggle to navigate. To mitigate this, researchers have proposed a novel approach that involves splitting this vast space into smaller, manageable parts and processing them separately. We have developed a system to implement this concept, where we break down the configuration space based on the system's runtime behavior and introduce a new tool to analyze these breakdowns and optimize the configuration settings. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach, showing that it significantly reduces the configuration space and improves performance by up to 90% in specific scenarios, while also reducing compilation time. We envision that this technique will be useful in practice, enabling users to efficiently navigate even the largest configuration spaces. The associated code is available for public use.

Molecular simulations of biophysical systems are often hindered by barriers 
that prevent simulations from reaching equilibrium. Using enhanced sampling 
techniques, this issue can be overcome by temporarily removing these obstacles 
and introducing 'guidance forces' that steer the system towards underexplored 
regions. However, the complexity of the system and the scale of the energy 
landscape make it difficult to obtain accurate data. To address this challenge, 
a new method has been developed that uses adaptive reinforcement learning to 
efficiently and accurately sample complex systems. This method has been applied 
to a model protein system, demonstrating its effectiveness in efficiently sampling 
the energy landscape and identifying key transition pathways compared to existing 
techniques. The success of this method highlights its potential as a powerful tool 
for understanding the intricate energy landscapes of biophysical systems. The 
flexibility and portability of this method make it a valuable addition to the 
enhanced sampling toolkit. The accompanying code and documentation are available 
on GitHub at https://github.com/AROMA-v2/FRD. The AROMA framework, which 
implements the FRD method, is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/AROMA-v2/AROMA.

The spread of misinformation poses a significant threat to democratic institutions and societal cohesion, necessitating research into its mitigation. A recent study has shown that exposing individuals to opposing viewpoints can counteract the influence of biased news consumption, leading to increased polarization. In response, we developed an optimization model to design social networks that minimize polarization while adhering to specific constraints. This model considers the potential for opposing opinions to 'backfire', influencing individuals' perceptions in the opposite direction. Our results indicate that the most effective networks often diverge from those predicted by models assuming a linear relationship between exposure and polarization. Furthermore, we found that networks designed to minimize polarization under a linear relationship often remain suboptimal when accounting for the 'backfire' effect, highlighting the need for tailored approaches to foster greater ideological diversity and inclusivity. As video conferencing continues to rise in popularity, the need for high-quality video compression without compromising latency and resource availability has become essential. This paper introduces Gemino, a novel video compression system that leverages neural modeling to deliver high-quality video while minimizing the load on both client and server. By employing a hybrid approach that combines the effectiveness of neural and traditional video codecs, Gemino strikes an ideal balance between high-quality video and reduced bandwidth consumption. Moreover, Gemino's use of a novel neural model allows for the accurate reconstruction of video frames even in the presence of errors, which are commonly encountered in video conferencing due to network packet loss. Experimental results demonstrate that Gemino outperforms current state-of-the-art video codecs in terms of subjective quality and can reduce video bandwidth consumption by up to 6.5x while maintaining a low packet loss rate of 2.5%. A comprehensive evaluation of Gemino's performance under various network conditions further highlights its potential as a reliable solution for video conferencing applications. Our method transforms the complex task of manipulating cloth into a hidden representation.
This representation, called a Cloth Funnel, is a mathematical model that describes the geometric properties of a cloth and its potential transformations.
The Cloth Funfunct allows us to develop a flexible and efficient garment manipulation system that can be applied to various tasks such as grasping, manipulation, and re-tying.
Our system is capable of generalizing to unseen garments and manipulation tasks, and can be trained on a large dataset of simulated data.
Experiments demonstrate that Cloth Funnels achieve state-of-the-art performance in manipulating real-world garments and can be trained with significantly less data. Additionally, Cloth Funfunct enables the transfer of learned manipulation skills from simulated to real-world environments. This work presents a new approach to multi-purpose garment manipulation and provides a new representation for modeling the geometric properties of deformable objects. In a remote state estimation scenario, a legitimate receiver aims to accurately estimate the state of a linear dynamic system, while keeping it hidden from an eavesdropper. We investigate how to minimize the knowledge gain of the eavesdropper by designing the control inputs and public transmissions of the legitimate receiver. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, this problem has a single optimal solution which exhibits certain properties, and we introduce a novel algorithm to compute this solution. We also show that under different conditions, this algorithm may not be applicable, and in such cases, we propose alternative solutions that strike a balance between achieving the optimal solution and addressing the limitations that prevent the use of the first algorithm. We further extend our approach to a more complex scenario where the legitimate receiver's actions also impact the dynamics of the system, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical simulations. We also highlight the potential of using our approach to design secure control systems that can protect against known attacks. Ultimately, this research aims to lay the groundwork for the development of privacy-protected control systems that can safeguard sensitive information. The task of salient object detection aims to pinpoint the most visually prominent objects within an image. These segments are then used to train a salient object detection model that can identify visually salient objects within images. To further enhance the model's accuracy, we employ a technique called subitizing, which allows the model to learn from a maximum of three salient segments per image. Our approach is evaluated against leading methods in this field and outperforms them in terms of both accuracy and speed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model can be trained end-to-end using weak bounding box annotations alone, without the need for manual pixel-level annotation.
